The world's stock markets

Two American exchanges hold more value than the next 58 put together

About 48,000 companies are listed on the world's stock exchanges. A few hundred of them carry most of the value. This page maps where that value sits, how deep each country's market is compared with its economy, and what investors pay for a dollar of sales.

Which exchanges matter

The ranking depends on what you count. By value, New York's two exchanges are in a league of their own. By number of listings, Tokyo and Mumbai move up the table.

How big is each stock market compared with its economy?

Dividing a country's total market value by its GDP gives the "Buffett indicator", a rough measure of financial depth. India's market is now worth more than its whole year's GDP.

US, Saudi and Swiss markets are worth more than twice their GDP. India is above 100%

Market capitalisation of listed domestic companies, % of GDP. Economies with GDP ≥ $100B.

Source: Show:

Source: World Bank WDI CM.MKT.LCAP.GD.ZS (latest year 2019–2024, shown in tooltip); our figure is tracked market cap (CompaniesMarketCap, Oct 2026) ÷ 2024 GDP (World Bank). Hong Kong is far off the chart at ~1,100% (World Bank) because mainland companies list there.

What investors pay per dollar of sales

Market value divided by revenue (price-to-sales) shows how much the market pays for each dollar a company sells. Price-to-earnings does the same for profit.

Technology and healthcare companies are valued at about 4 times sales. Retail, transport and real estate, at under 1

Median market value ÷ revenue by sector, Forbes Global 2000 (2026)

Source: Forbes Global 2000 (2026): market value May 2026, revenue and profit for the latest fiscal year. P/E uses profitable companies only.

Kuwait, Singapore, Taiwan and the UAE pay the most per dollar of sales. The US and India are close behind

Median market value ÷ revenue by country, listed universe (≥25 companies with revenue)

Source: listed universe (market cap Oct 2026; revenue SEC CY2025 or CompaniesMarketCap TTM). Forbes Global 2000 (2026) for P/E: countries with ≥20 companies. India is highlighted.

How each country's stock market has performed

Each country's main stock index since its data begins. Markets started in different years, so pick a start year and every line is reset to 100 there: a line at 300 means the market tripled. Switch to US dollars to compare like with like, because inflation and falling currencies inflate local numbers.

Index performance

Source: Yahoo Finance month-end index closes (checked against official year-end 2024 closes for 12 indexes: all match). US$ conversion uses monthly average exchange rates from the US Federal Reserve (FRED H.10/G.5), and Yahoo Finance rates for the Indonesian rupiah, Argentine peso, Israeli shekel and Turkish lira (available from 2001–2005 only). Price indexes: dividends are not included.

Every market ranked by yearly growth

Annual growth = compound yearly change in the index from the start month to the latest close. Lighter bars began later than the chosen start year, so they cover a shorter period: compare them with care.

Do the world's markets move together?

Correlation of monthly returns between each pair of markets: 1 means they rise and fall together, 0 means no link. High correlation means owning many markets protects you less than you think.

Correlation between markets

Pearson correlation of monthly percentage changes in each main index (same data as above). Markets in the same region are grouped together. Months where either index has no data are skipped; pairs with fewer than 24 shared months are left blank.
